view: Asfara means that the morning or dawn becomes bright, clear, and luminous.
note: Qatāda also describes the dawn as coming on.

view: Dawn spreads its light before sunrise.
The morning's brightening clears darkness and makes visible objects appear.
Isfār denotes appearance or becoming visible; the cited verse uses sufūr for a woman appearing without her veil.
A shining face can be described with this word, including the radiant faces of 80:38.
Uncovering a woman's face offers a possible sense or derivation for safara or asfara.
The word may derive from sweeping darkness away, as a broom clears a house.
Al-Rāghib distinguishes safara, uncovering a physical covering, from asfara, a color becoming clear and bright.
Dawn casting darkness off its face is a metaphor for its brightening.
The prophetic instruction to pray fajr at isfār uses the word in the sense of evident light, after doubt about dawn has gone.
The Prophet's instruction to delay dawn prayer until it brightens is explained as praying after the light appears.
The Prophet's instruction about dawn prayer is alternatively explained as lengthening the prayer until sunrise approaches.
note: The two explanations differ over whether the delay precedes or occurs within the prayer.

view: The expression 'pray at isfār' can mean entering the dawn time.
The common or majority reading uses the quadriliteral asfara with alif.
Ibn al-Sumayqa or al-Sumayfi and ʿĪsā ibn al-Faḍl read the triliteral safara without alif; it is also a valid or dialectal form for dawn's brightening.
note: The reading is also explained as dawn removing darkness from its face.

view: A reading attributed to ʿĪsā ibn al-Faḍl and Ibn al-Sumayfi is written 'idhā asfara' in this note and likened to morning casting darkness off its face; Abū Ḥātim considers it weak.
A reading of the preceding night clause with idhā and hamzated adbara parallels idhā asfara; the codices of ʿAbd Allāh and Ubayy reflect that parallel.
Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī regards both readings of the preceding adbara as sound.
The brightening morning is a third object of the oath, coordinated with the moon and night clauses.
The 'when' of dawn is future-looking because dawn follows the night.
Some take the oaths as sworn by the Lord of the moon, night, and morning, because an oath may be made only by God.
The answer to the oath follows the morning clause.
Specifying dawn invites contemplation of its marvels and the ordered regularity of its many motions.
The second dawn is the sun's white glow beneath the red twilight; sunset proceeds from red to white to darkness, and sunrise reverses that order before the sun's disk appears.
Dawn's brightening signifies lights of spiritual illumination appearing in hearts.
Dawn is spirit-light fully illuminating a receptive, clear heart and removing its darkness, after the night of the lower self or ego recedes.
note: Both accounts also take the moon as the receptive, clear heart.

view: Sunrise illuminating darkness depicts knowledge and guidance arriving and dispelling confusion.
The morning's unveiling is set against the night's retreat; idbār reverses night's arrival while isfār describes dawn clearing.
The preceding 'nay' rebukes deniers and rebels, specifically rejecting claims that people can know the number of God's hosts or overcome them.
The oaths honor divine signs and direct reflection to God, who sustains all existence; they also emphasize the importance of the warning to humanity.
The preceding moon oath is explained as referring to the crescent after its third night.
Nature's manifestations point to the Hereafter and expose heedlessness; the Qur'an warns people to prepare, while evaders retain stubbornness as their excuse.
The moon's gradual phases answer why Judgment is delayed: humanity likewise advances through stages, and the Day arrives at God's appointed time when the universe's purpose is fulfilled.
note: The note cites 36:39 for the moon's phases.

view: The emphatic negation precedes the oath because the audience's denial is objectionable enough to be rejected before proof is offered.
The oaths substantiate the following claim by answering disbelievers who ask why the promised Judgment has not yet come.
God's signs follow a prescribed plan whose benefits only He knows, so justice will come at its appointed time despite demands for haste.
Night yielding to morning illustrates this world's darkness giving way to Judgment at its appointed time, as certainly as daily dawn arrives.
The daily alternation of night and dawn rehearses Judgment and continually offers sincere truth-seekers evidence of that Day.
The oath recalls other Qur'anic oaths by the moon and by the alternation of night and day.
